section.heading: 3.5. Higher-Order Derivatives
Higher-Order Derivatives
section.paragraph: The derivative $$f^{\prime}$$ of a function $$f$$ is also a function. As such, the differentiability of $$f^{\prime}$$ may be considered. Thus, the function $$f^{\prime}$$ has a derivative $$f^{''}$$ at a point $$x$$ in the domain of $$f^{\prime}$$ if the limit of the quotient
exists as $$h$$ approaches zero. In other words, it is the derivative of the first derivative.

The function $$f^{''}$$ obtained in this manner is called the second derivative of the function $$f$$ , just as the derivative $$f^{\prime}$$ of $$f$$ is often called the first derivative of $$f$$ . Continuing in this fashion, we are led to considering the third, fourth, and higher-order derivatives of $$f$$ whenever they exist. section.paragraph: Just as the derivative of a function $$f$$ at a point $$x$$ measures the rate of change of the function $$f$$ at that point, the second derivative of $$f$$ (the derivative of $$f^{\prime}$$ ) measures the rate of change of the derivative $$f^{\prime}$$ of the function $$f$$ . The third derivative of the function $$f$$ , $$f^{'''}$$ , measures the rate of change of $$f^{''}$$ , and so on.

In Chapter 4, we will discuss applications involving the geometric interpretation of the second derivative of a function. The following example gives an interpretation of the second derivative in a familiar role.

note.source_type: Applied Example 4. Acceleration of a Maglev
note.title: Applied Example 4. Acceleration of a Maglev
note.heading: Applied Example 4. Acceleration of a Maglev
note.paragraph: Refer to A Real-Life Example. The distance $$s$$ (in feet) covered by a maglev moving along a straight track $$t$$ seconds after starting from rest is given by the function $$s = 4t^{2}(0 \leq t \leq 10)$$ . What is the maglev’s acceleration at any time $$t$$ ?
note.heading: Solution
note.paragraph: The velocity of the maglev $$t$$ seconds from rest is given by
$$v = \frac{ds}{dt} = \frac{d}{dt}(4t^{2}) = 8t$$
The acceleration of the maglev $$t$$ seconds from rest is given by the rate of change of the velocity of $$t$$ —that is,
$$a = \frac{d}{dt}v = \frac{d}{dt}\left( \frac{ds}{dt} \right) = \frac{d^{2}s}{dt^{2}} = \frac{d}{dt}(8t) = 8$$
or $$8$$ feet per second per second, normally abbreviated $$8{ft} \slash \sec^{2}$$ .

Then the first derivative of $$I$$ at $$t = c$$ , $$I^{\prime}(c)$$ , where $$a < c < b$$ , gives the rate of change of $$I$$ at $$c$$ . The quantity

section.paragraph: measures the inflation rate of the economy at $$t = c$$ . The second derivative of $$I$$ at $$t = c$$ , $$I^{''}(c)$$ , gives the rate of change of $$I^{\prime}$$ at $$t = c$$ . Now, it is possible for $$I^{\prime}(t)$$ to be positive and $$I^{''}(t)$$ to be negative at $$t = c$$ (see Example 6). This tells us that at $$t = c$$ , the economy is experiencing inflation (the CPI is increasing) but the rate at which the CPI is growing is in fact decreasing. This is precisely the situation described by an economist or a politician who claims that “inflation is slowing.” One may not jump to the conclusion from the aforementioned quote that prices of goods and services are about to drop!

note.title: Applied Example 6. Inflation Rate of an Economy the Function
note.heading: Applied Example 6. Inflation Rate of an Economy the Function
note.paragraph: gives the CPI of an economy, where $$t$$ is measured in years, with $$t = 0$$ corresponding to the beginning of 2004.

list.item: Find the inflation rate at the beginning of 2010 $$\left( {t = 6} \right)$$ .
Show that inflation was moderating at that time.

note.heading: Solution

list.item: We find $$I^{\prime}{(t)} = - 0.6t^{2} + 6t$$ . Next, we compute $$I^{\prime}(6) = - 0.6{(6)}^{2} + 6(6) = 14.4$$ and $$I(6) = - 0.2(6)^{3} + 3(6)^{2} + 100 = 164.8$$ from which we see that the inflation rate is $$\frac{I^{\prime}(6)}{I(6)} = \frac{14.4}{164.8} \approx 0.0874$$ or approximately $$8.7\%$$ .

We find $$I^{''}{(t)} = \frac{d}{dt}{({- 0.6t^{2} + 6t})} = - 1.2t + 6$$ Since $$I^{''}(6) = - 1.2(6) + 6 = - 1.2$$ we see that $$I^{\prime}$$ is indeed decreasing at $$t = 6$$ , and we conclude that inflation was moderating at that time (Figure 17). The graph appears to level out briefly as it reaches the top right. The CPI of an economy is given by $$I(t)$$ .
